literal: Prince of Yangping, Prince of Jingzhao, Prince of Jiyin, Prince of Ruyin, Prince of Leliang, Prince of Guangping
idiomatic: The Princes of Yangping, Jingzhao, Jiyin, Ruyin, Leliang, and Guangping

literal: Emperor Jingmu had fourteen sons.
idiomatic: Emperor Jingmu fathered fourteen sons.

literal: Empress Gong bore Emperor Wencheng.
idiomatic: Empress Gong bore Emperor Wencheng.

literal: Consort Yuan of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince You of Yangping, Xincheng.
idiomatic: Consort Yuan of the Pepper Chambers bore Xincheng, Prince You of Yangping.

literal: Consort Wei of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince Kang of Jingzhao, Tui, and the Prince of Jiyin, Xiao Xincheng.
idiomatic: Consort Wei of the Pepper Chambers bore Tui, Prince Kang of Jingzhao, and Xiao Xincheng, Prince of Jiyin.

literal: Consort Yang of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince Ling of Ruyin, Tiansi.
idiomatic: Consort Yang of the Pepper Chambers bore Tiansi, Prince Ling of Ruyin.

literal: Prince Li of Leliang, Wanshou, and Prince Shang of Guangping, Luohou—their mothers are not recorded.
idiomatic: Wanshou, Prince Li of Leliang, and Luohou, Prince Shang of Guangping—both lack recorded mothers.

literal: Consort Meng of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince Kang of Rencheng, Yun.
idiomatic: Consort Meng of the Pepper Chambers bore Yun, Prince Kang of Rencheng.

literal: Consort Liu of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince Hui of Nan'an, Zhen, and Prince Kang of Chengyang, Changshou.
idiomatic: Consort Liu of the Pepper Chambers bore Zhen, Prince Hui of Nan'an, and Changshou, Prince Kang of Chengyang.

literal: Consort Murong of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince Jing of Zhangwu, Tailuo.
idiomatic: Consort Murong of the Pepper Chambers bore Tailuo, Prince Jing of Zhangwu.

literal: Consort Wei of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince Kang of Leling, Hu'er.
idiomatic: Consort Wei of the Pepper Chambers bore Hu'er, Prince Kang of Leling.

literal: Consort Meng of the Pepper Chambers bore Prince Jing of Anding, Xiu.
idiomatic: Consort Meng of the Pepper Chambers bore Xiu, Prince Jing of Anding.

literal: Prince Zhao, Shen, died young and left no biography; his mother is not recorded.
idiomatic: Prince Zhao Shen died young without a biography; his mother is not recorded.

literal: In old Wei the rear apartments of the crown prince had no formal ranks; when Gaozong took the throne, every Gongzong palace woman who had borne a son was styled of the Pepper Chambers.
idiomatic: Under the old Wei the crown prince's inner quarters had no formal titles; at Gaozong's accession every Gongzong consort who had borne a son was styled of the Pepper Chambers.

literal: Xincheng, Prince of Yangping, was enfeoffed in the third year of Tai'an and appointed General Who Pacifies the West.
idiomatic: Xincheng, Prince of Yangping, received his fief in Tai'an year 3 and was made General Who Pacifies the West.

literal: Later he was Director of the Inner Palace.
idiomatic: He later served as Director of the Inner Palace.

literal: He died; posthumous title You.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously titled Prince You.

literal: His eldest son Anshou inherited the title.
idiomatic: His eldest son Anshou succeeded to the title.

literal: Gaozu bestowed the name Yi.
idiomatic: Gaozu granted him the name Yi.

literal: By successive promotion he became Grand General of Huaiyuan Garrison, commander of military affairs on all three routes, and marched north to campaign.
idiomatic: He rose to Grand General of Huaiyuan Garrison and commander of the three northern routes on campaign.

literal: An edict summoned him to the capital and urged him on matters of war.
idiomatic: He was summoned to the capital and exhorted on the conduct of war.

literal: He replied: "One must rely on the temple's plans and make the Khan submit as at Weiqiao Bridge."
idiomatic: He answered, "We should trust the court's strategy and bring the khan to homage as at Weiqiao Bridge."

literal: The emperor sighed and said: "How bold the prince's words!"
idiomatic: The emperor sighed. "What bold words from the prince!"

literal: That is what I hope for.
idiomatic: That is exactly what I hope for."

literal: Before he set out he suffered his mother's death; an edict sent palace attendants to urge him with the metal-and-leather exhortation.
idiomatic: Before he marched he entered mourning for his mother; attendants were sent to urge him back to duty under the metal-and-leather rule.

literal: After the burial he set out and with Lu Rui gathered the generals of the three routes to decide the army's course.
idiomatic: Once the burial was done he took the field; with Lu Rui he convened the three-route commanders to fix the line of march.

literal: Thereupon the center route went out by Black Mountain, the east route toward the Shilu River, and the west route toward the Houyan River.
idiomatic: The center column crossed Black Mountain, the east column pressed the Shilu River, and the west column the Houyan River.

literal: The army crossed the Great Marsh and routed the Rouran.
idiomatic: Crossing the Great Marsh they shattered the Rouran.

literal: When Yi came to court, an edict said: "The prince's earlier words were not empty."
idiomatic: On Yi's return an edict read, "Your earlier boast was no empty boast."

literal: Later he was made inspector of Shuozhou.
idiomatic: He was later appointed inspector of Shuozhou.

literal: When Mu Tai, inspector of Hengzhou, plotted rebellion he sent envoys urging Yi to be their leader.
idiomatic: When Hengzhou inspector Mu Tai rebelled he sent messengers offering Yi the leadership.

literal: Yi secretly reported the matter; Tai and the rest were executed, and the emperor greatly praised him.
idiomatic: Yi reported in secret; Tai and his party were put to death, and the emperor richly rewarded him.

literal: In the first year of Jingming of Emperor Shizong he died as inspector of Qingzhou,[2] posthumous title Prince Zhuang.
idiomatic: In Shizong's Jingming year 1 he died in office at Qingzhou,[2] and was posthumously titled Prince Zhuang.

literal: The line passed to his grandson Zongyin; in Suzong's time, for killing his uncle he was sentenced to death and the fief was abolished.
idiomatic: The title passed to his grandson Zongyin; under Suzong he was executed for murdering his uncle and the fief was extinguished.

literal: Yi's younger brother Yan, styled Anle, was granted the rank Marquis of Guangling.
idiomatic: Yi's brother Yan, courtesy name Anle, was made Marquis of Guangling.

literal: As inspector of Liangzhou he memorialized asking to be made acting king to lend weight to his authority.
idiomatic: As Liangzhou inspector he asked to be made acting king so his authority would carry more weight.

literal: An edict said: "This may be called insatiable asking; the request does not accord."
idiomatic: The edict answered, "This is sheer greed—the request is denied."

literal: Transferred to inspector of Xuzhou, he fell gravely ill on reaching the province; the emperor ordered Xu Chengbai to ride post-haste to treat him.
idiomatic: Moved to Xuzhou, he fell gravely ill on arrival; the emperor sent Xu Chengbai by express relay to heal him.

literal: When the illness eased and Chengbai returned, the emperor said, "You are a true famous physician," and rewarded him with three thousand bolts of silk.
idiomatic: When Yan recovered and Chengbai returned, the emperor said, "You are a physician of name indeed," and gave him three thousand bolts of silk.

literal: Chengbai declined and asked to receive only one thousand.
idiomatic: Chengbai refused and asked for only one thousand.

literal: The emperor said: "The Odes say, 'When men of worth perish, the state is laid waste.'"
idiomatic: The emperor said, "The Odes say, 'When worthy men are lost, the state withers.'"

literal: By that reckoning, is it only three thousand bolts?"
idiomatic: "By that measure, would three thousand bolts be enough?"

literal: Such was the weight the emperor gave him.
idiomatic: So highly did the emperor value him.

literal: Later, when his birth mother Lady Lei died, he memorialized asking to leave office.
idiomatic: Later, when his birth mother Lady Lei died, he asked to resign his post.

literal: An edict said: "What the former prince's residual honor abhors is plain in the rites; in the late age rites decayed and this canon was sometimes abandoned.
idiomatic: The edict read, "The rites plainly say what a former prince's residual honor forbids; in late days that canon was often abandoned."

literal: As the marquis is a king's son, he should follow the residual-honor rule and may observe only the greater mourning."
idiomatic: "As a king's son you should follow residual honor and observe only the greater mourning period."

literal: Later he died as inspector of Yongzhou, posthumous title Marquis Kang.
idiomatic: He later died as Yongzhou inspector and was posthumously titled Marquis Kang.

literal: Yan was by nature cautious and pure; wherever he served he was incorrupt, kept no estates, and through four provincial governorships won praise—yet on the day he died there was not even a shroud for his corpse.
idiomatic: Yan was sober and careful, incorrupt in every post, and built no estates; through four governorships he won praise, yet the day he died his household could not furnish a burial shroud.

literal: His son Chang.
idiomatic: His son was Chang.

literal: Chang's younger brother Rong, styled Shu.
idiomatic: Chang's younger brother Rong, courtesy name Shu.

literal: Rong's appearance was very short and ugly, yet his martial valor surpassed others.
idiomatic: Rong was remarkably short and plain of face, yet fiercer in arms than most men.

literal: When Emperor Zhuang plotted to kill Erzhu Rong, Rong was made Direct-Gate General.
idiomatic: When Emperor Zhuang plotted Erzhu Rong's death, Rong was made Direct-Gate General.

literal: When Erzhu Zhao entered Luoyang, Rong hid among the people.
idiomatic: When Erzhu Zhao took Luoyang, Rong vanished into the crowd.

literal: Yan's younger brother Qin, styled Siruo.
idiomatic: Yan's brother Qin, courtesy name Siruo.

literal: He held the posts Director of the Secretariat, Right Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing, and Pillar of State, third rank.
idiomatic: He served as Director of the Secretariat, Right Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing, and Pillar of State of the third rank.

literal: Qin's complexion was especially dark, so people of the time called him the Black-Faced Vice Minister.
idiomatic: Qin's complexion was unusually dark, and men called him the Black-Faced Vice Minister.

literal: Qin debauched the wife of his cousin Li, née Cui; Censor-in-Chief Feng Hui impeached him, but he was pardoned.
idiomatic: Qin seduced his cousin Li's wife, née Cui; Censor-in-Chief Feng Hui impeached him, but an amnesty spared him.

literal: Soon after he was made governor of Sizhou.
idiomatic: He was soon made governor of Sizhou.

literal: Qin from youth loved learning and early won a fine reputation; people said: "Among the imperial clan, broadly speaking—Shou'an and Siruo."
idiomatic: Qin loved books from youth and won early fame; people said, "Among the royal house, take Shou'an and Siruo."

literal: In later years, though he grew weighty in rank, he could not correct or aid the state; men of judgment looked down on him.
idiomatic: In his later eminence he offered the court little counsel, and discerning men held him cheap.

literal: Qin once asked the Qingzhou man Gaosengshou to find a tutor for his son; when the tutor arrived he fled after only a few days.
idiomatic: Qin once asked Gaosengshou of Qingzhou to find his son a tutor; the man came, then fled within days.

literal: Qin reproached Gaosengshou.
idiomatic: Qin blamed Gaosengshou.

literal: Gaosengshou, by nature a jester, turned and said to Qin: "Ordinary men who stop eating die in seven days; this one lasted only five mornings before running off—he left food for faith, and plainly lacked something."
idiomatic: Gaosengshou, a born jester, shot back: "A man who stops eating dies in seven days; yours lasted five mornings and bolted—he chose faith over food, and plainly lacked something."

literal: Qin was deeply ashamed and from then treated guests somewhat better.
idiomatic: Qin flushed with shame and afterward treated guests a little more generously.

literal: Later he was made Duke of Works and enfeoffed Duke of Juping county.
idiomatic: He was later made Duke of Works and enfeoffed Duke of Juping county.

literal: He was killed at Heyin; posthumously given the yellow battle-axe, Grand Preceptor, and Grand Duke of the State.
idiomatic: He was killed at Heyin and posthumously granted the yellow battle-axe, Grand Preceptor, and Grand Duke of the State.

literal: His son Zixiao, styled Jiye.
idiomatic: His son Zixiao, courtesy name Jiye.

literal: Early he had a fine reputation; at eight years Minister of State Cui Guang saw him and marveled, saying, "The coming leader of the younger generation will surely be this boy."
idiomatic: He won early fame; at eight Minister of State Cui Guang marveled at him and said, "The next generation's leader will be this boy."

literal: His son Taixing inherited.
idiomatic: His son Taixing succeeded.

literal: Made Grand General of Chang'an Garrison, for corruption he was stripped of office and title.
idiomatic: As Grand General of Chang'an Garrison he was removed from office and title for corruption.

literal: Later he was Director of the Secretariat, restored to his former title, made commander of Tongwan Garrison, and re-enfeoffed in Xihe.
idiomatic: He was later Director of the Secretariat, restored to his former rank, made commander of Tongwan Garrison, and re-enfeoffed in Xihe.

literal: Later the garrison was changed to Xiazhou, and Taixing remained inspector.
idiomatic: When the post was renamed Xiazhou, Taixing stayed on as inspector.

literal: He was made Acting Commandant of the Guards.
idiomatic: He was appointed Acting Commandant of the Guards.

literal: At first, when Taixing fell ill, he asked Buddhist monks to perform rites and at once gave away all his goods, begging recovery—the rite was called the "Life-Scattering Fast."
idiomatic: When Taixing first fell ill he had monks perform rites and gave away his entire fortune to beg a cure—a feast he called the Life-Scattering Fast.

literal: After the fast the monks all dispersed; one monk was just asking for leftover food from the fast.
idiomatic: When the fast ended the monks scattered; one lingered, asking for leftovers.

literal: Taixing jested: "The fast food is gone; only wine and meat remain."
idiomatic: Taixing teased him: "The fast fare is spent—only wine and meat are left."

literal: The monk said: "I can eat those too."
idiomatic: The monk said, "I can eat those as well."

literal: So he brought out a dou of wine and a sheep's leg; the monk ate all and still said he was not full.
idiomatic: They brought a dou of wine and a sheep's leg; he ate everything and still claimed hunger.

literal: After he left, wine and meat were still there; going out the gate to pursue him, nothing was seen.
idiomatic: When he had gone, the wine and meat remained untouched; men chased him beyond the gate but found no one.

literal: Taixing then prayed before the Buddha that the visitor must be no ordinary man; if this illness were cured he would abandon his princely title and enter the Way.
idiomatic: Taixing prayed before the Buddha that such a visitor could not be ordinary; if he recovered he would surrender his title and take orders.

literal: Before long he recovered, then asked to become a monk; he memorialized more than ten times before permission came.
idiomatic: He soon recovered, petitioned repeatedly to become a monk, and after a dozen memorials was allowed.

literal: At that time Gaozu was campaigning south in the field; an edict ordered the crown prince on the eighth day of the fourth month to tonsure him and grant two thousand bolts of silk.
idiomatic: Gaozu was then campaigning in the south; the crown prince was ordered to tonsure him on the eighth day of the fourth month and grant two thousand bolts of silk.

literal: Having become a monk, he took the name Sengyi and lived on Mount Song.
idiomatic: As a monk he took the name Sengyi and dwelt on Mount Song.

literal: In the twenty-second year of Taihe he died.
idiomatic: He died in Taihe year 22.

literal: His son Ang, styled Bohui, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Ang, courtesy name Bohui, succeeded.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Cong, styled Weiqing, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Cong, courtesy name Weiqing, succeeded.

literal: Under Emperor Xiaojing he rose to Grand Marshal, Recorder of the Masters of Writing, governor of Sizhou, and inspector of Qingzhou.
idiomatic: Under Xiaojing he became Grand Marshal, Recorder of the Masters of Writing, governor of Sizhou, and inspector of Qingzhou.

literal: He died in the province; posthumously given the yellow battle-axe, Grand Tutor, and Duke of the State, posthumous title Wen.
idiomatic: He died in office and was posthumously granted the yellow battle-axe, Grand Tutor, and Duke of the State with the title Wen.

literal: [3]Cong was generous and measured, handsome of face, and carried himself with grave dignity; between gain and loss his color did not change.
idiomatic: [3]Cong was open-handed and even-tempered, handsome, and grave in bearing; fortune and misfortune alike left his face unchanged.

literal: By nature he was pure and frugal and kept no estates; on the day he died the house held no surplus wealth.
idiomatic: He lived plainly and built no estates; the day he died his household had nothing left.

literal: Ang's younger brother Zhongjing was by nature stern and harsh.
idiomatic: Ang's brother Zhongjing was severe by nature.

literal: In Emperor Zhuang's time he concurrently served as Censor-in-Chief, and the capital grew orderly.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Zhuang he also served as Censor-in-Chief, and the capital grew orderly.

literal: Whenever he went to the bureau he always drove a red ox, so people called him the Red-Ox Censor.
idiomatic: He always drove a red ox to the bureau, and men called him the Red-Ox Censor.

literal: At the beginning of Taichang he was Intendant of Henan and enforced the law without private favor.
idiomatic: Early in Taichang he was Intendant of Henan and enforced the law without favor.

literal: At that time Minister of Personnel Fan Zihe's subordinates ran rampant and also committed theft; Zhongjing secretly arrested and seized them all and at once executed them, so the powerful grew fearful.
idiomatic: Minister of Personnel Fan Zihe's men were running riot and stealing; Zhongjing seized them in secret, executed them on the spot, and the great families trembled.

literal: When Emperor Chu was about to go west, Zhongjing was made Grand Commander of the Central Army and left in the capital.
idiomatic: As Emperor Chu prepared to move west, Zhongjing was made Grand Commander of the Central Army and left to hold the capital.

literal: King Xianwu of Qi wished to reach Luoyang; Zhongjing then abandoned wife and children and fled.
idiomatic: When King Xianwu of Qi marched on Luoyang, Zhongjing deserted wife and children and fled.

literal: His son Chong inherited.
idiomatic: His son Chong succeeded.

literal: He had no sons; the fief was extinguished.
idiomatic: He left no sons, and the fief died out.
